source.title: Investigation of Training Label Error Impact on RNN-T
source.authors: I-Fan Chen; Brian King; J. Droppo

page_placements.theme: Corruption structure matters beyond its rate

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some PDF text extraction has line breaks and minor formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests label-error effects in RNN-T speech recognition and finds distinct effects by error type, contradicting a broad assumption that label corruption behaves uniformly. It does not test random image-label memorization itself.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for simulated deletion, insertion and substitution errors and several mitigation settings. It does not test fully random labels, chance-level test error, training time to fit noise, unstructured inputs, or whether real patterns are learned before noise. No row for V6: the discussion of prior work is cited background, not this study's result.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out ASR word error after structured transcription corruption at 1–6% word-level error rates. It reports neither memorization of corrupted training labels nor training-fit trajectories. Its regularization and scaling experiments address ASR degradation, and its discussion of learning real patterns before noise cites prior work. These results do not test V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that deletion transcription errors are especially harmful to RNN-T ASR and recommend prioritizing their reduction. Tested mitigation approaches do not eliminate the clean/noisy performance gap. Their fixed-dataset experiments leave dynamically updated self-learning datasets unresolved; fixed does not mean that training-data size was never varied.
record.recipe_differences: The study simulates transcription deletion, insertion and substitution errors in 5k-hour far-field ASR data and measures relative word error rate in RNN-T systems. It does not use random image labels or the original image-classification setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with error type and rate; deletion errors have greater reported WER impact than substitution or insertion. Regularization type, training-data size and model size also change reported performance.

fits_no_version.finding: At 6% word-level label error, held-out WER increases by 9.2% for deletions, 3.1% for substitutions, and 0.4% for insertions relative to clean training. At 1%, substitution and insertion instead slightly improve WER.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of simulated transcription corruption on RNN-T generalization depends on error type and rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout and SpecAugment separately improve held-out WER on clean and corrupted data; SpecAugment improves it more. Corrupted-data models retain a gap from their corresponding clean-data models. Combining the methods provides no additional gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization improves RNN-T ASR performance without eliminating the tested transcription-error penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing data from 5k to 80k hours improves both clean and deletion-corrupted systems while their performance gap persists. Increasing model size from x1 to x2 helps all systems; x2 to x6 provides no further improvement for corrupted systems while clean systems continue improving.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data and model scaling have limited ability to compensate for the tested transcription errors in RNN-T ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: Oracle filtering leaves 77.2% of utterances. Relative WER worsens from 0.645 to 0.683 for substitution and from 0.630 to 0.684 for insertion, but changes from 0.699 to 0.697 for deletion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization trade-off from removing corrupted utterances depends on transcription-error type; the reported deletion benefit is numerically small and has no uncertainty estimate.

record.problems: The study uses de-identified in-house far-field ASR data and does not disclose absolute WER values. It reports relative metrics without uncertainty estimates. Some size-scaling findings are presented only as curves in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Rows report R WER only; other error-type metrics in Tables 3 and 6 were not extracted because they are additional ASR outcome measures unrelated to the six claim versions.

untested.parts: Completely random training labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and fitting without architecture or hyperparameter changes.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence speed as corruption increases. Training until convergence does not establish either.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit throughout a random-label corruption sweep and steadily increasing test error toward chance. The structured, low-rate transcription errors and held-out WER measurements do not establish this behavior.

Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label memorization, and whether removing it makes true-label generalization poor. The reported WER improvements from regularization do not establish either proposition.
Temporal ordering of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing noise. No corresponding training trajectories are reported.

record.verdict_notes: All reported relative error values use b0 absolute WER as their normalization denominator; other baseline entries can identify comparison systems. Different effects of structured transcription errors do not contradict any listed version, which does not assert uniform effects across error types. No claim-version verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests simulated transcription errors, not completely random labels, zero training error, test error at chance, or unchanged training settings versus true labels.
Training time or convergence speed as a function of label corruption is not reported.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.
The study evaluates ASR performance under selected label error types and rates; it does not report perfect training fit or a smooth test-error trajectory from clean labels to fully random labels.

Regularization is evaluated for mitigating ASR degradation, but the study does not test whether regularization prevents fitting random labels or whether its removal alone harms generalization on true labels.
The study does not measure the order in which real patterns and label errors are learned. Its remarks on that topic cite prior work.

relation.reason: The introduction discusses prior findings on memorization and learning shared patterns first; the experiments address transcription-error impact and mitigation rather than those findings.

tranche.reason: The study measures held-out ASR degradation under structured transcription corruption, without measuring training-label memorization, fitting speed or learning order. Its own results test none of V1–V6.

source_check.notes: R WER values are ratios to b0, not absolute WER percentages; absolute WER is withheld. The authors’ conclusion paraphrase is consistent with the text: fixed datasets exclude dynamic self-learning, while dataset size was varied.
